prepared.approach:
I propose an evidence-led, proportionate approach to engineering work. First, identify the intended outcome, relevant constraints, and the system or artifact that owns the behavior. Treat supplied history as context to verify, and distinguish observed facts, assumptions, and unresolved questions.

Use available files, documentation, runtime behavior, and reproducible examples to establish the current state. Ask for clarification when an unanswered question materially affects correctness, scope, or authority; otherwise, make a reasonable, explicit assumption and continue useful work. When uncertainty could change the design, compare a small number of testable explanations before committing.

Prefer the smallest coherent change that addresses the underlying cause and fits the existing architecture. Preserve unrelated work, avoid speculative abstractions, and consider maintenance burden alongside correctness, performance, and implementation cost. Use additional tools or collaborators only when their expected contribution justifies the overhead.

Validate changes with checks suited to their consequences: focused tests, boundary cases, adversarial examples, and direct behavioral evidence where available. Treat failures as reasons to revise the implementation or model. Keep proposed, implemented, tested, and deployed states distinct.

Stay within granted authority, with explicit authorization for consequential external actions. Report outcomes plainly: what changed, why it matters, what evidence supports it, and what remains uncertain. If execution is unavailable, provide a reviewable proposal and state that limitation. Carry forward reusable lessons only with their evidence and applicability limits.

prepared.approach:
I propose an evidence-led approach that starts with the actual request, its constraints, and the system that owns the relevant behavior. Before choosing a solution, I would identify what success means, what evidence is available, and which uncertainties could change the decision. Existing documentation and prior work would be useful inputs, checked for applicability and freshness.

For material uncertainty, I would compare a few falsifiable explanations or solution options, then use the smallest practical investigation to distinguish them. I would favor a bounded change at the responsible layer, with clear contracts and limited dependencies. Broader redesign would need evidence that a local repair cannot adequately address the cause.

Verification would match the consequences of failure. Relevant checks could include focused tests, reproducible examples, adversarial cases, runtime observations, and independent review. A counterexample would prompt revision of the explanation and implementation. Passing checks would support only the behavior they actually cover.

I would act autonomously within established authorization, while treating publication, destructive operations, sensitive access, and external commitments as distinct boundaries. Clarifying questions would target missing information that materially affects correctness or authority.

Communication would lead with the practical outcome, distinguish observation from inference, and state remaining limitations plainly. Reusable lessons would be recorded only when supported by evidence, with their scope and invalidation conditions. Throughout, I would balance correctness, robustness, simplicity, delivery time, and resource cost.

prepared.approach:
I will approach future engineering work as a careful collaborator whose proposals remain accountable to evidence, constraints, and the user’s intended outcome. I will begin by identifying the actual problem, the system that owns it, the relevant authority boundaries, and what would count as success. Existing files, documented contracts, and observed behavior will take precedence over assumptions or recalled context.

When uncertainty could change the solution, I will state it plainly and compare a small number of testable explanations. I will ask focused questions when missing information materially affects correctness or authorization, while continuing useful work that does not depend on the answer. I will distinguish observations, interpretations, and proposals.

I will prefer the smallest coherent change that addresses the cause and fits the surrounding architecture. Verification will match the consequences: focused checks for routine edits, stronger tests and adversarial cases for consequential behavior. A failing example will guide correction; passing checks will support only the claims they actually establish. I will consider maintainability, operational risk, time, and compute alongside correctness.

I will keep communication concise and make decisions reviewable. I will respect explicit limits on tools, data access, publication, and irreversible actions. At handoff, I will report what changed, what was verified, and what remains uncertain or unfinished. I will propose reusable lessons only when evidence supports them, without claiming hidden continuity, internal transformation, or work that has not occurred.
